Font audit · Unicode coverage · Arabic specimen

Al-Fātiḥah font coverage report

Analysis of 54 font files supplied in fonts.tar.gz. This page includes the rendered specimens, the coverage findings, and copyable CSS unicode-range declarations.

Executive summary

54font files inspected
16full Al-Fātiḥah coverage (31/31)
2partial coverage
36no Arabic specimen coverage
Key finding: 54 files were inspected. 16 can map every character used in this Al-Fātiḥah specimen, 2 are partial, and 36 have no Arabic glyph coverage. The 36 unsupported files are Noto Serif Bengali styles; they should not be used as Arabic fallback fonts.

Partial fonts: KacstBook.ttf is missing U+0653, U+0670 and U+0671. KFGQPC Uthman Taha Naskh Regular.ttf is missing U+0671. Browsers will normally source those characters from a later fallback font, so a line can appear mixed even when most letters come from the selected face.

Coverage means the font’s best Unicode character map (cmap) contains the required code point. It does not prove that every mark is positioned ideally, that Qur’anic ligatures are identical to a printed muṣḥaf, or that tajwīd/recitation is validated.

What the CSS unicode-range should do

unicode-range tells the browser which Unicode code points are eligible to use a particular @font-face. It does not add missing glyphs. The declarations below are generated from each font’s actual best cmap and compressed into contiguous ranges.

For example, the browser can use a Qur’anic font for Arabic code points and a separate font for Bengali text. Keep each face’s range tied to the characters that font actually maps; then order your font-family fallback list intentionally.

@font-face {
  font-family: 'ArabicQuranFont';
  src: url('./fonts/YourArabicFont.ttf') format('truetype');
  font-style: normal;
  font-weight: 400;
  font-display: swap;
  unicode-range: U+0600-06FF, U+0750-077F, U+08A0-08FF;
}

.quran-text {
  font-family: 'ArabicQuranFont', 'Noto Naskh Arabic', serif;
  direction: rtl;
  unicode-bidi: plaintext;
  font-synthesis: none;
}

The three broad ranges above are an illustration only, not a recommendation for every font. Use the per-file exact ranges in the tables below. The HTML preview images are self-contained; the CSS snippets point to ./fonts/, so place the original font files in a folder named fonts beside the stylesheet or edit the paths.

OpenType shaping indicators

For Arabic, the presence of joining-form substitutions and mark-positioning features is useful evidence that the font is intended to shape Arabic text. It is not a guarantee that every browser/engine will produce identical Qur’anic typography.

  • Joining: look for GSUB features such as isol, init, medi, and fina.
  • Marks: GPOS features such as mark and mkmk position vowel marks relative to base letters and other marks.
  • Qur’anic glyphs: some fonts contain specific Qur’anic characters or ligatures. Character coverage alone cannot tell you whether the desired Madani/IndoPak glyph style is correct.

Each specimen card lists the common shaping features detected in its GSUB/GPOS tables. The full feature tags are also present in the underlying font metadata, but are not repeated for all 54 fonts here.

Font embedding metadata note

The font binaries are not embedded in this report. The visible specimen images are static renderings, and the CSS declarations reference the original local files. This avoids repackaging the supplied font binaries in the report.

  • _PDMS_Saleem_QuranFont Regular.ttf: fsType 0x0004 — Preview/print only bit · Vendor terms / other.
  • Al Qalam Quran Majeed Web Regular.ttf: fsType 0x0004 — Preview/print only bit · No licence string in name table.
  • DigitalKhattIndoPak.otf: fsType 0x0008 — Editable embedding bit · OFL 1.1.
  • MUHAMMADI QURANIC FONT.ttf: fsType 0x0006 — Restricted embedding bit; Preview/print only bit · No licence string in name table.

The OS/2 fsType field is technical metadata, not a substitute for reading each font’s licence. Confirm the font vendor’s terms before serving the original file from a public website.

Method and limitations

  • Inspected 54 TTF/OTF files using the best Unicode cmap, glyph inventory, OS/2 embedding flags, and GSUB/GPOS feature tags.
  • Generated each exact Unicode range by collapsing contiguous code points from that font’s cmap. Gaps are preserved; unsupported characters are not silently included.
  • Rendered specimen previews in Chromium on Linux using the exact source fonts. Appearance can differ slightly in other browsers, operating systems, and font-shaping engines.
  • Text set: Uthmani/Hafs rendering of Al-Fātiḥah, based on the Arabic text published by Sajadah (which attributes the Arabic text to Quran.com).
  • This is a technical font-coverage and visual-comparison report, not a religious text verification or a tajwīd assessment.
